premises.text: People fail at saving because hardwired impulse instincts meet retail environments, wasting 10–20% of disposable income, while budget/spreadsheet approaches do not work
premises.evidence_span: spending between 10 and 20% of our disposable income on these silly purchases we don't need

premises.text: ImpulseSave creates an FDIC-insured interest-bearing piggy bank linked to checking with personal savings goals
premises.evidence_span: create an online piggy bank, a savings account that's FDIC-insured and interest-bearing

premises.text: In the moment of an impulse buy, users can redirect the would-be spend into savings via mobile app (and later scan/SMS/Instagram/on-site)
premises.evidence_span: have the amount she was just about to have spent be transferred automatically in that moment into her ImpulseSave savings account

premises.text: Optional social sharing of impulse saves and behavioral/location notifications market users' own goals back to them
premises.evidence_span: close to 40% of our users choose to share their impulse saves

premises.text: Users save substantial amounts (about $3,000/year on average for savers; ~2 saves/week at ~$15)
premises.evidence_span: our savers are saving over $3,000 a year right now

value.text: Make saving as easy and instantly gratifying as spending, toward goals that matter
value.evidence_span: made it just as easy and as instantly gratifying to save your money as it is to spend it

causal_links.evidence_span: why do we suck so bad at it?
You just saved $25 towards your trip to Paris
we're going to use our ninja marketing skills to market those to you

notes: Hunting/gathering + retail predation + budget failure folded as one behavioral problem set (§4.1.6). Multi-channel save methods (app/SMS/Instagram/on-site) folded as cascade of the redirect-to-save mechanism (§4.1.7). Matching funds future incentive noted as near-future—not coded as separate premise. Usage averages treated as continuing efficacy condition with the product.
